name: London
description: The world's greatest football city, with six Premier League clubs and countless lower-league sides spread across its boroughs.
longDescription: London is unlike any other football city in the world. From the Emirates in North London to Craven Cottage by the Thames, from Stamford Bridge in Fulham to the London Stadium in Stratford, the capital offers football fans an unparalleled choice of clubs, stadiums, and matchday experiences. With world-class transport links, iconic landmarks, and some of Europe's finest hotels and restaurants, a football trip to London is genuinely special.

bestAreas.name: Central London (Soho / Covent Garden)
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: Tube access to all clubs; 20-40 min to any ground
bestAreas.description: For fans visiting multiple stadiums, or those who want the full London experience with football as one element of the trip, Central London is the obvious base. Soho and Covent Garden are 20-40 minutes by tube from any Premier League ground in the city. The choice of hotels is staggering — from budget chains to five-star institutions — and the restaurants, bars, and cultural life within walking distance are unmatched. The compromise is cost: central London hotels are expensive, and you're never exactly close to any stadium.
bestAreas.recommendation: The Rosewood on High Holborn is one of London's great hotels — a Belle Époque court building with some of the best food in the city.

bestAreas.name: King's Cross / Islington
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 3-min tube to Arsenal; 20-min tube to Spurs; 35-min tube to Chelsea
bestAreas.description: The area around King's Cross has been dramatically regenerated — Coal Drops Yard, Granary Square, and the increasingly vibrant streets around the station make this one of London's most interesting places to stay. For Arsenal fans it's unbeatable: the Piccadilly line takes you to Arsenal station in three minutes. Islington, just south, has some of the best independent restaurants in London and a genuinely local feel. Hotels range from budget chains near the station to some handsome boutique options in Islington itself.
bestAreas.recommendation: The Megaro Hotel directly opposite King's Cross has excellent rooms and a brilliant basement bar — and you're three minutes from Arsenal.

bestAreas.name: Westfield Stratford / Olympic Park
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 5-min walk to London Stadium; 40-min tube to Arsenal/Chelsea
bestAreas.description: The area around the Olympic Park in Stratford is the best base for West Ham fans and a genuine destination in its own right. The Westfield shopping centre is enormous, the Elizabeth line makes the rest of London accessible in minutes, and the hotels here are modern, well-priced, and genuinely convenient. The London Stadium is a five-minute walk. If the Hammers are at home and you want to be right there without paying central London prices, Stratford is the obvious answer.
bestAreas.recommendation: The Westfield Stratford City hotels (AC, Staybridge, and others) are reliable and walk-distance from the stadium.

bestAreas.name: Chelsea / Fulham / South Kensington
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 10-min walk to Stamford Bridge or Craven Cottage
bestAreas.description: Staying in Chelsea or Fulham puts you within walking distance of two Premier League grounds — Stamford Bridge and Craven Cottage are both reachable on foot from the Kings Road. This is one of the most expensive and pleasant parts of London: the restaurants on Fulham Road are excellent, the pubs around Parson's Green are old and proper, and the neighbourhood feels very different from other parts of the city. Hotels are fewer and more expensive than elsewhere, but the convenience for Chelsea and Fulham fans is unmatched.
bestAreas.recommendation: The Sydney House Chelsea on Sydney Street is a small, beautifully decorated boutique hotel — one of London's finest small hotels.

bestAreas.name: Seven Sisters / Tottenham
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 10-min walk to Tottenham Hotspur Stadium
bestAreas.description: For the dedicated Spurs fan who wants to be right in the thick of the north London atmosphere, Seven Sisters and the surrounding area provides budget accommodation options close to the ground. The Tottenham High Road on match day is one of London's most visceral football experiences — street food, flags out, the whole neighbourhood in motion. It's not a glamorous part of London and the hotel choices are limited, but there's something genuinely authentic about staying in the area around the stadium rather than making the journey from the west end.
bestAreas.recommendation: White Hart Lane station (the nearest Overground stop) has a couple of decent guesthouses within a few minutes' walk.

intro: No city on earth offers what London does for the football fan. Seven Premier League clubs — more than any other city in the world — spread across the greatest metropolis in Europe, each with their own distinct identity, neighbourhood, and story. The Emirates sits in working-class north London; Stamford Bridge in expensive, quiet Fulham; the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium rising from the terraced streets of N17; Craven Cottage perched on the Thames bank like a Victorian folly; the London Stadium in the transformed Olympic Park of Stratford. Each ground is a portal into a different London — different accents, different pubs, different reasons for loving the game. The city's tube network makes it possible to attend a morning fixture at one end of London and be back in the West End for dinner without a car or a plan. London is also, of course, one of the world's great cities in every other dimension: the museums, the restaurants, the parks, the architecture. Football here is one layer of a very deep cake, but it's a layer that runs through everything — from the stadium tours to the scarves in the market stalls to the ex-players running pubs in south London. Give it time. It rewards you.
matchDayGuide: Match day in London is as varied as the city itself, and entirely dependent on which club you're visiting. At the Emirates, the walk from Arsenal tube is short and glorious — Holloway Road fills with red and white from 90 minutes before kick-off. At the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, the approach from White Hart Lane station through the Tottenham High Road gives you proper north London atmosphere. At Stamford Bridge, the Kings Road and Fulham Road create a very different social world — a wealthier, quieter crowd that still generates real noise in the ground. At Craven Cottage the Thames setting is genuinely beautiful; at the London Stadium in Stratford the modern Westfield complex creates an almost shopping-centre feel before you enter. The golden rule across all of them: London crowds are not slow. Arrive a full 90 minutes before kick-off if you want a pre-match drink and a comfortable entrance. The tube gets extremely busy in the hour before kick-off at any major London fixture, and platforms fill quickly. After the match, the city simply absorbs the crowd — you're never far from a pub, a restaurant, or a route home.

preMatchPubs.name: The Tollington Arms
preMatchPubs.description: The pre-match pub of choice for Arsenal fans on Hornsey Road. Fills fast on big days — arrive at least 90 minutes before kick-off. Proper boozer, no frills, excellent atmosphere.

preMatchPubs.name: The Pembury Tavern
preMatchPubs.description: A Wetherspoon, yes, but one of the best-positioned pre-match options in the Tottenham area. Large capacity means you can usually get a drink even an hour before kick-off. Mixed crowd of home and away fans.

preMatchPubs.name: The Cock Tavern
preMatchPubs.description: One of the better pubs near Stamford Bridge on Fulham Road. Gets very busy on match days but the beer is good and the atmosphere is warm. The surrounding Fulham Road pubs are all worth trying.

preMatchPubs.name: The Supporters Club, Olympic Park
preMatchPubs.description: The West Ham supporters' club operation near the London Stadium. Ticket holders only on match days, but if you're a member the pre-match setup here is excellent — proper West Ham atmosphere in a modern setting.

restaurants.name: Ottolenghi, Islington
restaurants.description: One of London's most influential restaurants — Yotam Ottolenghi's original Islington spot. The mezze-style sharing plates are perfect for a pre-match lunch near Arsenal. The deli counter breakfasts are also superb.

restaurants.name: Piebury Corner
restaurants.description: An Arsenal institution — proper pies, close to the Emirates, open from midday on match days. Don't queue for food inside the stadium at half-time when this exists.

restaurants.name: Hawksmoor Seven Dials
restaurants.description: The best steak in London, in a beautiful converted townhouse. For a special dinner in the city centre the night before a big match. The Sunday roast is also legendary.

restaurants.name: Padella
restaurants.description: Brilliant fresh pasta at extremely reasonable prices. There's always a queue but it moves fast and the food is worth every minute. Perfect for a pre-match lunch in south London if you're heading to Crystal Palace or Millwall.

postMatch.name: Coal Drops Yard
postMatch.description: The converted Victorian coal dropping facility behind King's Cross has some of London's best bars and restaurants. Perfect for Arsenal and Spurs fans making their way back through the city — Barrafina, Dishoom, and several excellent independent bars.

postMatch.name: Dishoom
postMatch.description: The Bombay café concept with sites in King's Cross, Covent Garden, Carnaby, and Shoreditch. Great for post-match dinner regardless of result — the black dal and bacon naan are the antidote to a bad afternoon.

postMatch.name: The American Bar at The Savoy
postMatch.description: For the ultimate post-match splurge in the most theatrical setting in London. Art Deco perfection, outstanding cocktails, and the kind of ambience that makes everything feel more significant. Dress accordingly.

gettingAround.fromAirport: London has five airports and all are well connected. From Heathrow (LHR): the Elizabeth line (Crossrail) runs directly to Paddington, Bond Street, Liverpool Street, and beyond — 25 minutes to central London. From Gatwick (LGW): Gatwick Express to Victoria in 30 minutes. From Stansted (STN): Stansted Express to Liverpool Street in 47 minutes. From City Airport (LCY): Elizabeth line to central London in 25 minutes. Taxis from Heathrow are expensive (£60-90 to central London) — use public transport unless time is the primary factor.
gettingAround.fromStation: London has multiple mainline termini — Euston, King's Cross, Paddington, Victoria, Waterloo, Liverpool Street — and all connect directly to the Underground. From whichever station you arrive at, buy an Oyster card or use contactless payment for all tube and bus travel: it's the most efficient and cheapest way to navigate the city. The tube will get you to any Premier League ground in London within 40 minutes of any mainline station.
gettingAround.betweenStadiums: The Underground makes multi-stadium visits genuinely feasible. Arsenal to Chelsea takes around 45 minutes (Piccadilly line to District line). Spurs to Arsenal takes about 20 minutes on the Victoria or Piccadilly lines. Chelsea to Fulham is walkable (about 25 minutes along the Thames, or a short bus ride). The Elizabeth line has transformed east-west travel — Stratford (West Ham) to Paddington now takes under 20 minutes. Plan your tube route on Citymapper rather than the TfL website; it handles the match day crowd surges better.
gettingAround.localTransport: The Tube is everything. Get an Oyster card or use contactless (bank card or phone) from the moment you arrive — never buy single paper tickets, which are significantly more expensive. The daily cap on Oyster/contactless means unlimited travel after a certain spend. Buses are excellent for travelling within zones 1-2, and far cheaper for short journeys. Taxis (black cabs or Uber) are abundant but expensive in central London. On match days, the tube gets extremely crowded in the 60 minutes before kick-off — try to travel 90 minutes early to avoid the worst crush.

beyondFootball.name: The British Museum
beyondFootball.description: Free entry to one of the world's great museums — the Rosetta Stone, the Elgin Marbles, Egyptian mummies, Lindow Man. You cannot see it all in a day and shouldn't try. Pick a civilisation and go deep. The Great Court is also one of the finest architectural spaces in London.

beyondFootball.name: Borough Market
beyondFootball.description: London's greatest food market under the arches of London Bridge. Saturday morning before an afternoon match at Chelsea, Arsenal or Fulham is the perfect combination — an hour at Borough Market (try the Kappacasein toasted cheese, the Monmouth coffee, the Ethiopian injera) and then the tube out to the stadium.

beyondFootball.name: A Sunset Walk Along the South Bank
beyondFootball.description: From Tate Modern past Shakespeare's Globe, under the Millennium Bridge, past the Tate Modern, along Bankside to Borough Market, across Tower Bridge, and back along the north bank. London's most reliably spectacular walking route, and it's entirely free. Do it at dusk.

beyondFootball.name: The National Gallery, Trafalgar Square
beyondFootball.description: One of the world's great collections of Western European painting, free to enter. The Sunflowers are here. So are the Caravaggios, the Vermeers, and the Turner Rooms. Even a single hour spent here is one of the best things you can do in London.

beyondFootball.name: Wembley Stadium Tour
beyondFootball.description: The home of English football offers behind-the-scenes tours that include the royal box, the dressing rooms, and the famous tunnel. For serious football fans, standing in the tunnel with Abide With Me playing through the PA is worth the entry price alone.

beyondFootball.name: Notting Hill and Portobello Road Market
beyondFootball.description: On Friday and Saturday mornings, the Portobello Road antiques and food market is one of London's great spectacles. The surrounding streets of Notting Hill are some of the most beautiful in the city. It's a very different London from the football grounds, which is exactly why it's worth doing.

insiderTips: Arsenal tube station is on the Piccadilly line and is literally named after the club — it's the only station in London named after a football club, and it's a three-minute walk from the Emirates. There is no closer tube-to-stadium relationship in London.

For Spurs, White Hart Lane on the Overground (not to be confused with the old name of the stadium) is actually marginally better than Seven Sisters tube for avoiding the main crowd crush after the game.

Craven Cottage has no tube station directly — Putney Bridge (District line) is the closest at 15 minutes on foot, or take the Putney bus from Hammersmith. The Thames-side walk to the stadium is one of the most pleasant pre-match approaches in English football.

London hotel prices spike massively on Premier League weekends, particularly for Arsenal and Chelsea home matches. Book as far in advance as possible — three to four months for major fixtures. Mid-week matches offer dramatically better hotel rates.

The Elizabeth line (Crossrail) has genuinely changed London — journey times from east to west are now dramatically shorter. Stratford to Paddington in 18 minutes means West Ham is no longer 'inconveniently east' for visitors staying in the centre.

name: Manchester
description: Home to two of the world's most famous clubs, Manchester is England's second football city and a brilliant destination.
longDescription: Manchester has two of the most famous clubs on the planet — United and City — and a football culture that runs through the city's veins. Old Trafford, the Theatre of Dreams, sits in Trafford, while the Etihad Stadium has transformed East Manchester. The city centre itself is buzzing with culture, great food, and nightlife. Whether you're here for a Premier League blockbuster or just soaking in the football atmosphere, Manchester never disappoints.

bestAreas.name: City Centre / Northern Quarter
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 20-min tram to Old Trafford; 20-min tram to Etihad
bestAreas.description: The ideal base for fans visiting either club. The Northern Quarter is Manchester's most interesting neighbourhood — independent bars, record shops, street food, and some of the best coffee in the North. The Metrolink tram runs from St Peter's Square to Old Trafford (Trafford Bar stop) and from Piccadilly Gardens toward the Etihad (Velopark/Etihad Campus stops). Hotels in the city centre vary enormously — the Gotham on King Street is the premium choice, while Ancoats has some excellent boutique options.
bestAreas.recommendation: The Stock Exchange Hotel in Norfolk Street is one of the most remarkable hotels in England — a converted Victorian trading floor with extraordinary rooms.

bestAreas.name: Salford Quays / MediaCityUK
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 10-min walk or tram to Old Trafford; 25-min tram to Etihad
bestAreas.description: Salford Quays has transformed from industrial wasteland into a genuine destination — the Lowry theatre, MediaCityUK, and a cluster of waterfront bars and restaurants make it one of the most interesting places to stay in Greater Manchester. For United fans it's unbeatable: Old Trafford is a ten-minute walk across the canal. The tram also connects you quickly to the city centre. Hotels here are modern, usually well-priced, and the waterfront setting is genuinely attractive on a crisp match day morning.
bestAreas.recommendation: The Lowry Hotel overlooks the Irwell and has hosted visiting teams for decades — if you want to feel like a player, this is the one.

bestAreas.name: Ancoats
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 15-min walk or tram to Etihad; 30-min tram to Old Trafford
bestAreas.description: Manchester's most fashionable neighbourhood and the best base for City fans. Ancoats was a Victorian cotton-milling district that's been completely reimagined — Michelin-starred restaurants, excellent coffee bars, and boutique accommodation in converted mills. It's walkable to the Etihad on a match day and the area has a genuine community feel that the city centre can lack. For United fans it's less convenient but the food and drinks scene here is the best in Manchester.
bestAreas.recommendation: Culturally it's the most interesting place to stay in the city — base yourself here if you want Manchester beyond the football.

bestAreas.name: Deansgate / Castlefield
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 25-min tram to Old Trafford; 25-min tram to Etihad
bestAreas.description: Deansgate is Manchester's grandest street — Victorian warehouses and modern bars side by side, running from the city centre down to Castlefield's Roman fort and canal basins. The area has excellent hotels and a good choice of restaurants. Castlefield itself is one of Manchester's hidden gems: the amphitheatre and canal-side bars around Bridgewater Canal are outstanding on a summer match day. For travel purposes, Deansgate tram stop connects to both stadiums.
bestAreas.recommendation: Great John Street Hotel is a converted Victorian school — small, individual, and genuinely charming.

bestAreas.name: Stretford / Old Trafford
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 5-10 min walk to Old Trafford; 35-min tram to Etihad
bestAreas.description: If you're going to a United match and want to be completely immersed, staying in the streets around Old Trafford puts you right in the thick of it. Hotels and guesthouses in Stretford are budget-priced and limited, but the experience of waking up and walking to the ground on match day — past the Sir Alex Ferguson statue, under the Munich Clock, through the crowds — is something city-centre hotels simply can't offer. Not glamorous, but for a pure United fan experience it's unbeatable.
bestAreas.recommendation: Sir Matt Busby Way itself has a couple of hotels close to the forecourt — ideal for the full theatre of arrival.

intro: Manchester is a city that invented modern football and has never stopped living it. Two of the world's most recognised clubs share the same city — Old Trafford to the south-west, the Etihad to the east — and the rivalry between them runs through the city like electricity through a cable. But Manchester's football identity is about more than United and City. This is the place that gave the world the Football League, that sent clubs across Europe on their earliest adventures, that produced some of the game's most iconic moments. The city itself has always been restless and self-reinventing: the post-industrial landscape that produced Joy Division and the Haçienda gave way to the regenerated Northern Quarter, to Ancoats with its Michelin-starred restaurants, to Salford Quays with its media empire and waterfront hotels. Walk down Deansgate on a Saturday when both clubs are at home and the city is two separate worlds sharing one skyline — red here, blue there, and a sharp edge between them. It's one of the most genuinely exciting football cities in the world, and one that repays repeated visits far more than most.
matchDayGuide: A Manchester match day has its own distinct geography depending on which club you're visiting. For United, the day starts around Old Trafford — the pubs on Sir Matt Busby Way and Warwick Road begin filling from midday, and the walk from Manchester city centre (or Salford Quays tram stop) through the terraced streets of Stretford has its own slow-building theatre. For City, the Etihad district has transformed beyond recognition — the Sportscity complex and the cluster of bars around the stadium create a pre-match village that didn't exist a decade ago. The City of Manchester Stadium has the kind of modern facilities that make match day comfortable, but the atmosphere in the away end — steep, tight, atmospheric — is excellent. For both clubs the principle is the same: arrive early, pick a pub, get involved. Manchester pubs near football grounds are among the best in England — proper boozers with genuine matchday energy, not tourist-facing operations. And after the game, win or lose, the Northern Quarter and Deansgate absorb the crowds and keep things going well into the night.

preMatchPubs.name: The Bishop Blaize
preMatchPubs.description: The closest pub to the Old Trafford entrance and perennially packed on match days. Gets loud and brilliant from two hours before kick-off. Arrive early or face a very long queue at the bar.

preMatchPubs.name: The Trafford Bar
preMatchPubs.description: More relaxed than the Bishop Blaize and a decent alternative if you want a seat. Good for a pint and a pie before heading to the ground.

preMatchPubs.name: The Townley, Ardwick
preMatchPubs.description: The best pre-match pub for City fans — a proper neighbourhood boozer that heaves on match days with knowledgeable, passionate City fans. The away end crowd tends to drink here too.

preMatchPubs.name: Sinclair's Oyster Bar, Shambles Square
preMatchPubs.description: A 500-year-old timber-framed pub that was physically relocated to make way for the Arndale — one of Manchester's great historical oddities, and one of its best old pubs. Worth knowing about if you're drinking in the city before heading out.

restaurants.name: Mana
restaurants.description: The only Michelin-starred restaurant in Manchester. Nordic-influenced tasting menu in a stripped-back warehouse setting. Book months in advance. A proper occasion restaurant for the night before a big match.

restaurants.name: Elnecot
restaurants.description: Modern British cooking in a gorgeous old mill building. Brilliant for dinner the night before — the Sunday roast is also exceptional if you're staying for the weekend.

restaurants.name: Bundobust Manchester
restaurants.description: Indian craft beer and street food — the Manchester outpost of the Leeds original. Great bhaji, excellent beer, and a brilliantly casual pre-match format.

restaurants.name: Hawksmoor Manchester
restaurants.description: The finest steak in Manchester, in one of the most beautiful converted Victorian dining rooms in the country. Expensive and worth it for a celebratory dinner.

postMatch.name: Bunny Jackson's
postMatch.description: Dark, loud, and brilliant — a Northern Quarter bar with a great whisky list and late licence. The post-match choice for those who want the night to continue.

postMatch.name: The Refuge
postMatch.description: Gorgeous Arts and Crafts bar inside the former Refuge Assurance building. The most beautiful post-match drink in Manchester — whether you're celebrating or drowning sorrows, the setting helps.

postMatch.name: Albert's Schloss
postMatch.description: A Bavarian beer hall with live music and a late licence. Enormous fun on a match day evening — the crowd is always mixed and the atmosphere is reliably excellent.

gettingAround.fromAirport: Manchester Airport (MAN) is 9 miles south of the city and exceptionally well-connected. The Metrolink tram runs directly from the airport to the city centre (around 50 minutes, stopping at Piccadilly). Trains also run from Manchester Airport station to Manchester Piccadilly (around 20 minutes, more expensive). Taxis take 25-35 minutes to the city centre and cost around £25-35. For Old Trafford direct from the airport, the Metrolink is simplest — change at Cornbrook for Trafford Bar.
gettingAround.fromStation: Manchester Piccadilly is the main arrival station and is directly connected to the Metrolink network. For Old Trafford, take the tram toward Altrincham/Sale and alight at Trafford Bar (20 minutes, then 10-min walk). For the Etihad, the dedicated Etihad Campus tram stop is served by Ashton-under-Lyne and Droylsden line services (around 20 minutes from Piccadilly). Manchester Victoria station is also central and connects to the Metrolink.
gettingAround.betweenStadiums: Old Trafford and the Etihad are 5 miles apart with no direct tram link — you need to go via the city centre. The most practical route on match day is tram to Piccadilly (or Victoria), then change for the other stadium. Journey time is around 35-45 minutes door to door. Taxis between the stadiums cost around £15-20 but traffic on match days can be severe. The city centre itself is the natural midpoint for any multi-stadium day.
gettingAround.localTransport: The Metrolink tram network is the key to Manchester's match day transport — reliable, affordable, and running late. Get an app-based ticket (or tap-in with contactless) rather than queuing at machines. Taxis are readily available throughout the city. Avoid driving on match days near either stadium — parking is severely restricted and the surrounding roads gridlock badly.

beyondFootball.name: The Football Museum, Cathedral Gardens
beyondFootball.description: The national museum of English football sits in the city centre and is free to enter. Even for obsessive fans there'll be things here they haven't seen — the original Football League tables, early FA Cup balls, the kit collections. A must for any serious football tourist.

beyondFootball.name: Kelham Island Museum (Sheffield equivalent — try MOSI)
beyondFootball.description: The Museum of Science and Industry on Liverpool Road tells the story of Manchester's industrial revolution in fascinating detail — steam engines, textile machinery, and the world's first railway passenger station. It's the context that explains the whole city.

beyondFootball.name: The Whitworth Art Gallery
beyondFootball.description: One of Britain's finest regional art galleries, set in Whitworth Park south of the city centre. The building — a converted Victorian institution dramatically extended in 2015 — is as impressive as the collection. Free entry.

beyondFootball.name: The Northern Quarter
beyondFootball.description: Even if you're not shopping, a wander through the Northern Quarter's independent record shops, vintage clothes stores, and coffee bars is the best way to understand what makes Manchester's cultural identity so distinct. Tib Street and Oldham Street are the twin axes.

beyondFootball.name: Castlefield and the Roman Fort
beyondFootball.description: Manchester was a Roman fort — Mamucium — and the reconstructed walls in Castlefield are surprisingly atmospheric. The surrounding canal basin has some of Manchester's best outdoor bars, particularly in summer. The Bridgewater Canal towpath is a lovely walk west toward Old Trafford.

beyondFootball.name: Old Trafford Cricket Ground
beyondFootball.description: One of England's great Test match venues sits adjacent to the football stadium. If there's cricket on during your visit, a session at Old Trafford (the cricket one) is a very fine way to spend a morning — the contrast between the intimacy of a county ground and the scale of Old Trafford football is striking.

insiderTips: The Metrolink tram is the non-negotiable way to get to both stadiums on match days. Buy a return before you go out — queues at tram stops after a game can be long, and having a ticket ready saves time.
For United, the Old Trafford South Stand tram stop (Trafford Bar) is the correct stop, not 'Old Trafford' which is actually closer to the cricket ground. Easy mistake to make.

The Manchester Derby (United vs City) is among the hardest tickets in world football. Both clubs have points-based ballot systems — register with both as early as possible and accumulate points by attending other fixtures.
Ancoats is where to eat — not the tourist-facing restaurants around Piccadilly Gardens or Deansgate. Get a reservation at Elnecot or Mana before you arrive. They book up weeks in advance.
The Northern Quarter gets very busy on Saturday nights — if you're celebrating after a match, get to a bar by 9pm to guarantee entry. Several venues have no-queue policies for groups who book ahead.

name: Liverpool
description: Home to two legendary clubs sharing the same park, Liverpool is a passionate football city with incredible culture.
longDescription: Liverpool is one of England's great football cities. Anfield and Goodison Park sit just across Stanley Park from each other, making Liverpool unique in hosting two major clubs so close together. The city itself is warm, welcoming, and packed with culture — the Merseyside accent is the friendliest in England. From the Albert Dock to the Beatles Story, from the incredible cathedral to the buzzing pub scene, Liverpool is a brilliant destination whether you're supporting the Reds or the Blues.

bestAreas.name: City Centre / Ropewalks
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 25-min taxi or match day shuttle to Anfield
bestAreas.description: The obvious base for visiting fans and the right choice for most people. Ropewalks is Liverpool's entertainment district — Bold Street, Seel Street, and Mathew Street all within walking distance, surrounded by excellent bars and restaurants. The match day shuttle bus to Anfield runs from several stops nearby. Hotels on Dale Street and Victoria Street offer the best balance of price and location; most major chains have a presence here. The Albert Dock is an easy 15-minute walk, and you're central enough to everything the city has to offer without paying waterfront premiums.
bestAreas.recommendation: The Aloft Liverpool on North John Street is well-positioned and reliably good for match weekends.

bestAreas.name: Liverpool Waterfront / Albert Dock
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 25-min taxi to Anfield
bestAreas.description: Staying on the waterfront puts you in the most scenic part of the city. The Albert Dock — a UNESCO World Heritage Site — is surrounded by boutique hotels, the Tate Liverpool, the Merseyside Maritime Museum, and some of the city's best restaurants. It's about a mile from the city centre and not walkable to either stadium, but taxis are plentiful. If comfort and atmosphere matter as much as proximity to football, this is where you want to be. The views over the Mersey at dusk, particularly in winter, are genuinely spectacular.
bestAreas.recommendation: The Titanic Hotel in nearby Stanley Dock is a converted Victorian warehouse — one of the great football weekend hotels in England.

bestAreas.name: Anfield
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 5-10 min walk to Anfield
bestAreas.description: If you want to be as close as possible to the ground, the streets immediately around Anfield have B&Bs and guesthouses at budget prices. It's not the most scenic part of Liverpool — the area is still going through regeneration — but the walk to the stadium on match day is something else entirely: flags out of windows, chippies open from noon, fans streaming in from every direction. The experience of waking up on match day already in the thick of it has a genuine appeal that no city-centre hotel can match.
bestAreas.recommendation: Book early — there's limited accommodation right around Anfield and it sells out fast on big fixtures.

bestAreas.name: Baltic Triangle
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 30-min taxi to Anfield
bestAreas.description: Liverpool's creative quarter has emerged as one of the city's most interesting neighbourhoods over the past decade. Converted warehouses turned into bars, street food courts, and independent venues give it a distinctly cool energy that the city centre proper can't match. It's slightly south of the centre and you'll be using taxis for the stadium, but the Baltic Triangle rewards those who want something beyond the standard hotel experience. Camp and Furnace and the Invisible Wind Factory are both enormous event venues worth knowing about if you're staying a few nights.
bestAreas.recommendation: The Baltic Hotel is a well-run boutique option right in the middle of the action.

bestAreas.name: Wirral / Birkenhead
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 40-50 min (ferry + taxi)
bestAreas.description: For serious budget travellers, crossing the Mersey to stay in Birkenhead or New Brighton can cut hotel costs by 40-50% compared with Liverpool city centre. The Merseyrail network gets you back into Liverpool in 15-20 minutes, and the Mersey Ferry itself — immortalised in song — is a Liverpool experience in its own right. It's not for everyone: the transport adds complexity, and late nights mean a longer journey back. But if you're on a tight budget, the Wirral is a genuinely practical alternative and the views of Liverpool's skyline from the ferry are unforgettable.
bestAreas.recommendation: Birkenhead Central is the best-connected station for getting back to Liverpool quickly after a late match.

intro: Liverpool hits you differently to other football cities. The moment you step off the train at Lime Street and feel the salt air off the Mersey, there's a warmth and confidence here that you don't get anywhere else in England. It's a city that knows it's special — and isn't shy about it. Home to two of English football's most storied institutions, Liverpool and Everton sit barely a mile apart on either side of Stanley Park, creating a football density unique in world football. The people are the real draw. Scousers have an easy humour, a fierce local pride, and a genuine warmth towards visitors that makes even away fans feel — briefly — at home. Walk into any pub on a match day and you'll be in conversation with strangers within five minutes. The city has reinvented itself multiple times — maritime powerhouse, Beatles capital, European City of Culture — but football has been the constant. What's remarkable is how naturally the city wears all of it. The regenerated waterfront, the extraordinary Georgian architecture, the world-class music venues: none of it feels performative. Liverpool is simply, gloriously itself — and for football fans, there is nowhere quite like it.
matchDayGuide: On a match day in Liverpool, the electricity starts building from mid-morning. The pubs along Walton Breck Road and Anfield Road begin filling from midday — earlier for European nights or title-run-in fixtures. The walk from the city centre up through Everton Valley is itself an experience: streets lined with flags and scarves, pie vans steaming on corners, the low murmur of the city growing louder as you get closer. By the time you turn the corner and see the Main Stand's great curving roof over the rooftops, the hairs on your neck stand up regardless of your allegiance. Around the ground, the pre-match pubs — the Sandon, the Albert, the Arkles — have been hosting fans for decades and they fill fast. Get there at least 90 minutes before kick-off if you want a pint and a seat. The Kop begins to fill steadily from an hour before kick-off; by the time the players emerge the noise is something physical. After the game, win or lose, the city absorbs it and bounces back. The bars on Bold Street, Castle Street, and Hope Street stay busy until well past midnight — Liverpool is very much a late city.

preMatchPubs.name: The Sandon
preMatchPubs.description: The spiritual home of Anfield pre-match drinking. Once the pub where Liverpool FC was literally founded in 1892, now a sprawling, chaotic, brilliant boozer that heaves on match days. Arrive at least two hours before kick-off.

preMatchPubs.name: The Albert
preMatchPubs.description: Long-standing Anfield local with no-frills decor, proper pub atmosphere, and a crowd that's been coming here for decades. One of the most authentic match day pub experiences in English football.

preMatchPubs.name: The Arkles
preMatchPubs.description: Popular with home and away fans alike — one of the friendlier mixed pubs near the ground. Good beer, reasonable prices, and a lively pre-match atmosphere without feeling threatening.

preMatchPubs.name: The Philharmonic Dining Rooms
preMatchPubs.description: If you're starting your match day in the city, this Victorian masterpiece on Hope Street is unmissable. One of the most ornate pub interiors in Britain. Go for the architecture as much as the beer.

restaurants.name: Mowgli Street Food
restaurants.description: Brilliant Indian street food in a casual, buzzy setting on Liverpool's most interesting eating street. Ideal for a pre-match lunch that won't leave you uncomfortable in your seat.

restaurants.name: The Art School
restaurants.description: Liverpool's premier destination restaurant from chef Paul Askew. Elegant, expensive, and worth every penny for a special occasion dinner. Book well in advance.

restaurants.name: Bundobust
restaurants.description: Indian craft beer bar and street food. Combine a couple of interesting beers with excellent bhaji and chaat — a perfect pre-match format.

restaurants.name: Salt House Tapas
restaurants.description: The best tapas in Liverpool, consistently. If you're in the city the night before a match, this is the dinner booking to make. The pork belly pintxo is essential.

postMatch.name: Alma de Cuba
postMatch.description: A converted Polish church turned into an over-the-top bar with Latin music and cocktails. Ridiculous in the best possible way — perfect for celebrating a win with a group.

postMatch.name: Buyers Club
postMatch.description: The best late bar in Liverpool — rotating DJs, a relaxed crowd, and good drinks. The post-match spot for those staying in the city who want the night to continue.

postMatch.name: Camp and Furnace
postMatch.description: A vast converted warehouse in the Baltic Triangle that becomes a club and events venue on weekends. Worth the taxi if you want a proper night out.

gettingAround.fromAirport: Liverpool John Lennon Airport is 9 miles south of the city. The Arriva 500 express bus runs to the city centre every 30 minutes (around 40 minutes journey time, £4 single). Taxis take 20-25 minutes and cost around £20-25. There is no direct rail link. For Anfield direct from the airport, a taxi is £25-30 and takes 30-35 minutes — often the most practical option if you're arriving on match day.
gettingAround.fromStation: Liverpool Lime Street sits right in the city centre and is the gateway to everything. From here to Anfield by taxi takes 25-30 minutes and costs around £12-15 — or take the match day shuttle bus, which runs directly from the city centre to Anfield on game days. Goodison Park is similarly 20-25 minutes from Lime Street.
gettingAround.betweenStadiums: Anfield and Goodison Park are barely a mile apart — easily walkable in 20 minutes through Stanley Park. The park route between the two grounds is a lovely walk and gives you a sense of just how tightly the city's football geography is packed. On a dry day it's the only sensible way to travel between them.
gettingAround.localTransport: Merseyrail is excellent for reaching the wider Liverpool city region. Within the city and to the stadiums, taxis are plentiful and reasonably cheap — most journeys under £15. The match day shuttle bus to Anfield is the easiest option on game days; it runs from several city centre pick-up points and drops right outside the ground. Avoid driving on match days — parking around Anfield is extremely limited and the surrounding streets fill up hours in advance.

beyondFootball.name: The Albert Dock
beyondFootball.description: Liverpool's most iconic waterfront development houses the Tate Liverpool, the Merseyside Maritime Museum, and the Beatles Story — all under one roof on a regenerated Victorian dock. Walk it on a Saturday morning before a match and you'll understand why this city is so proud of its waterfront heritage.

beyondFootball.name: The Two Cathedrals Walk
beyondFootball.description: Hope Street connects two extraordinary cathedrals — the Gothic Anglican Cathedral (the largest in Britain) and the modernist Metropolitan Cathedral at the other end. The walk between them, through the Georgian Quarter, is one of the finest short urban strolls in England.

beyondFootball.name: Crosby Beach — Antony Gormley's Another Place
beyondFootball.description: Eight miles north of the city, 100 life-size cast iron figures by sculptor Antony Gormley stand in the tidal sands, gazing out to sea. One of the most haunting and brilliant public artworks in Britain — and it's free, and accessible, and unforgettable. Get there at dusk if you can.

beyondFootball.name: The Mersey Ferry
beyondFootball.description: The iconic Mersey Ferry — immortalised by Gerry and the Pacemakers — crosses between Liverpool Pier Head and Birkenhead. It takes an hour in total, costs almost nothing, and the views back over the Liverpool skyline are spectacular. A genuine city experience that's easy to overlook.

beyondFootball.name: Anfield Stadium Tour
beyondFootball.description: Even if you're not a Liverpool fan, the stadium tour is worth doing. The history on display — the Shankly philosophy, the Hillsborough memorial, the European nights — is genuinely affecting. The tunnel experience under the main stand is particularly atmospheric.

beyondFootball.name: The Cavern Quarter and Mathew Street
beyondFootball.description: Not the Beatles-themed tourist trap it sounds — the Cavern Club is still a functioning music venue and Mathew Street itself has a certain gritty authenticity. On a Friday or Saturday night the whole quarter is heaving. At least have one drink in the original Cavern on the basis that you should.

insiderTips: Book the match day shuttle bus in advance for Liverpool FC fixtures — it sells out. Alternatively, get a taxi and ask to be dropped at the junction of Walton Breck Road and Anfield Road: perfect position for the pre-match pubs.
The away end at Anfield (the Anfield Road End) has some of the best sight lines in the Premier League. If you're going as a neutral or away fan, they're well worth having.
Liverpool is a genuinely late city — pubs don't empty until well past midnight on match weekends. If you've got an early train home the morning after, set multiple alarms.

The Merseyside Derby is among the hardest tickets in English football. Apply to both clubs' official ballot systems at least six months in advance — and don't bother with touts, the prices are extortionate.

Goodison Park may not be around for much longer — Everton are moving to their new stadium at Bramley-Moore Dock. If it's still standing during your visit, make every effort to get to a game. It's one of the last authentic old English grounds, and once it's gone, it's gone.

name: Birmingham
description: England's second city is home to Aston Villa and Birmingham City, with great transport links and a fantastic food scene.
longDescription: Birmingham is England's second city and a brilliant football destination. Aston Villa's Villa Park is one of the country's most historic grounds, steeped in tradition. The city has undergone a major transformation in recent years with fantastic restaurants, bars, and cultural attractions. The Grand Central shopping centre and Brindleyplace are highlights. With great train connections from London (just 90 minutes) and a welcoming local culture, Birmingham makes for a great matchday trip.

bestAreas.name: City Centre
bestAreas.description: The ideal base with direct trains to Witton for Villa Park. Excellent hotels and dining.

bestAreas.name: Jewellery Quarter
bestAreas.description: Trendy area with boutique accommodation. Easy access to the city centre and Witton.

bestAreas.name: Brindleyplace
bestAreas.description: Canal-side area with upscale hotels near the ICC.

name: Newcastle upon Tyne
description: One of England's most passionate football cities, Newcastle is famous for its Geordie culture and the iconic St James' Park.
longDescription: Newcastle is quite simply one of the most football-mad cities in England. St James' Park sits right in the heart of the city centre — you can see it from miles around — and the Geordie faithful are among the most passionate supporters in the country. The city itself is brilliant: the Quayside is one of the most vibrant urban waterfronts in England, Jesmond is a lovely leafy suburb with great restaurants, and the nightlife is legendary. Newcastle is genuinely one of the best away-day destinations in the Premier League.

bestAreas.name: City Centre
bestAreas.description: Steps from St James' Park. Grey Street has beautiful Georgian architecture and excellent hotels.

bestAreas.name: Quayside
bestAreas.description: The most atmospheric part of Newcastle. Boutique hotels with river views.

bestAreas.name: Jesmond
bestAreas.description: Residential suburb with independent restaurants and B&Bs. Easy Metro access to the stadium.

name: Brighton & Hove
description: England's coolest seaside city, Brighton is a fantastic destination for football with the Amex Stadium on its doorstep.
longDescription: Brighton is genuinely one of the best destinations for a football trip in England. The Amex Stadium in Falmer is modern and easy to reach, and the city itself is one of the most vibrant, creative, and welcoming places in the country. The seafront is spectacular, the Lanes are full of independent shops and cafés, and the food scene is exceptional. Whether you're visiting for a Premier League match or a trip to the coast, Brighton never disappoints.

bestAreas.name: City Centre / North Laine
bestAreas.description: The best base. Direct train to Falmer on match days. Huge hotel choice.

bestAreas.name: Seafront
bestAreas.description: Classic Brighton experience. Hotels with sea views and easy access to the city.

bestAreas.name: Hove
bestAreas.description: Quieter and more residential. Good value hotels and easy links to Brighton station.

name: Glasgow
description: Scotland's largest city and the home of the greatest club rivalry in world football — Celtic vs Rangers.
longDescription: Glasgow is Scotland's greatest football city and one of the best in Britain. Celtic Park and Ibrox Stadium are iconic grounds that generate some of the most incredible atmosphere in world football. The Old Firm rivalry between Celtic and Rangers is unlike anything else in sport. But Glasgow is much more than football — it's a genuinely exciting city with world-class museums, a thriving music scene, excellent restaurants, and some of the friendliest people you'll ever meet. Don't miss the West End, the Merchant City, and the incredible Kelvingrove Art Gallery.

bestAreas.name: City Centre / George Square
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 20-min bus/taxi to Celtic Park; 20-min subway/taxi to Ibrox
bestAreas.description: The city centre is the natural base for visitors to Glasgow — central, well-connected, and surrounded by the best restaurants and bars the city has to offer. George Square is the civic heart, ringed by Victorian buildings and a short walk from Central and Queen Street stations. The Subway (Glasgow's excellent underground network) connects the city centre to Ibrox in minutes; buses and taxis cover Celtic Park. The hotel choice here is the widest in the city, covering all price points from budget chains to premium hotels.
bestAreas.recommendation: The Kimpton Blythswood Square Hotel occupies a handsome Georgian building on the square of the same name — Glasgow's best hotel, and worth the splurge.

bestAreas.name: Merchant City
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 20-min bus to Celtic Park; 25-min subway to Ibrox
bestAreas.description: Glasgow's most fashionable neighbourhood sits just east of the city centre — a grid of Georgian and Victorian warehouses converted into bars, restaurants, and boutique hotels. The bar scene here is the best in the city: Hutchesons, Paesano, and Bar 91 are all excellent. On weekends the Merchant City buzzes from mid-afternoon into the small hours, making it one of the most enjoyable places to be on a match day evening. It's slightly less convenient than the city centre proper but makes up for it in atmosphere and food quality.
bestAreas.recommendation: Mono on Kings Court is a legendary vegan bar and music venue — don't be put off by that description, it's one of the best pubs in Glasgow.

bestAreas.name: West End / Hillhead
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 30-min bus to Celtic Park; 15-min subway to Ibrox
bestAreas.description: The West End is Glasgow at its most architecturally beautiful — the grand Victorian terraces of Hillhead and Dowanhill, Byres Road lined with independent bars and restaurants, the Botanic Gardens at the top. It's a residential and university neighbourhood with a very different atmosphere from the city centre: quieter, more relaxed, excellent for an evening meal before or after a match. The Subway from Hillhead to Ibrox is direct. For Celtic, you'll need a bus or taxi. Hotels are fewer and more boutique-scale but the area rewards staying here.
bestAreas.recommendation: The Alamo Guest House on Gray Street is a much-loved B&B in the heart of the West End — book early, as it sells out fast.

bestAreas.name: Govan / Ibrox
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 5-min walk to Ibrox; 30-min subway to Celtic Park
bestAreas.description: For Rangers fans who want to be in the thick of it, Govan puts you right next to Ibrox. The area has a proud industrial history — the Clyde shipyards that built the Empire's greatest ships were launched from here — and the community around the stadium is warm and welcoming to visiting fans. Budget guesthouses and the occasional small hotel provide affordable options. The walk from Govan subway station to the stadium on match day is everything you'd want from a football experience: flags, scarves, the ground materialising above the rooftops.
bestAreas.recommendation: The Ibrox area has limited hotel stock — book well in advance for big matches, as options fill quickly.

bestAreas.name: Finnieston / Anderston
bestAreas.distanceToStadium: 25-min taxi to Celtic Park; 15-min taxi to Ibrox
bestAreas.description: Finnieston has become Glasgow's most talked-about neighbourhood over the past decade — the 'Fin' strip on Argyle Street has more good restaurants per square mile than almost anywhere in Scotland. It sits between the city centre and the Clyde, with excellent connections west toward Ibrox and a vibrant eating and drinking scene that's perfect for a match-day evening. Hotels are appearing here as the neighbourhood's reputation grows. Slightly further from both stadiums than other options, but the food scene alone justifies the choice.
bestAreas.recommendation: The Ox and Finch on Sauchiehall Street is one of Scotland's best restaurants — sharing plates, exceptional wine list, and buzzy atmosphere.

intro: Glasgow is the most intense football city in Britain, and one of the most intense in the world. This is where the Old Firm was born — where Celtic and Rangers have been locked in a rivalry so total, so encompassing, that it has shaped not just the football culture but the social fabric of the city for over a century. To understand Glasgow is to understand the rivalry: Catholic and Protestant, Irish immigrant and Scottish establishment, green and blue. It is a divide that has softened at the edges over generations but remains the organising principle of Scottish football life. What surprises first-time visitors is how little this rivalry dims the warmth of the city itself. Glaswegians — all of them, both sides — are among the most genuinely hospitable people in Britain. The city has one of the best restaurant and bar scenes outside London, a music culture that has punched far above its weight for fifty years, and an architectural heritage that makes walking the city a continual pleasure. The Merchant City, the West End, the Clyde waterfront: Glasgow repays the visitor who looks beyond the football. But the football is why most people come, and it is magnificent — raw, passionate, extraordinarily atmospheric in a way that the sanitised Premier League can rarely match.
matchDayGuide: Match day in Glasgow is an experience that no other British city can replicate. For a Celtic match, the walk up to Celtic Park through Parkhead starts hours before kick-off — the pubs on London Road fill from noon and the sense of occasion builds steadily, crescendoing into one of the loudest welcomes in European football when the teams emerge. The Bhoys' support has a choral quality — the songs are old, the melodies familiar, and when 60,000 voices join together the effect is deeply moving regardless of your affiliation. For a Rangers match, the approach to Ibrox through Govan is different but equally impressive — the red-brick stadium rising over the tenement streets, the blue and white scarves, the noise on Bill Struth Main Stand. The Old Firm itself is something else entirely. The city divides along invisible lines, the pre-match atmosphere crackles with a tension that is genuinely unlike anything in English football, and the match itself — fast, physical, emotionally loaded — rarely disappoints as a spectacle. One rule applies for all Glasgow fixtures: respect the colours. The city is safe and welcoming, but Old Firm match day is not the moment to explore the other side's territory in the wrong shirt.

preMatchPubs.name: The Brazen Head, London Road
preMatchPubs.description: A long-standing pre-match institution for Celtic fans on London Road. Gets extremely busy from 90 minutes before kick-off. One of the most atmospheric Celtic pubs in the city — green-scarved, loud, and genuinely welcoming to visiting fans.

preMatchPubs.name: The Sarry Heid (Saracen's Head), Gallowgate
preMatchPubs.description: One of Glasgow's oldest pubs, reportedly dating from 1755. Dark, historic, atmospheric — more a pilgrimage than a pre-match drink, but a pub that anyone with an interest in Glasgow's history should visit at least once.

preMatchPubs.name: The Louden Tavern, London Road
preMatchPubs.description: A Rangers pub on London Road — incongruously positioned near Celtic Park but serving an entirely different clientele. Proof that Glasgow football pubs are not geographically determined. Welcoming and atmospheric.

preMatchPubs.name: The Shed Bar, Ibrox
preMatchPubs.description: The most straightforward pre-match option for Rangers fans — directly beside the stadium, busy from 2 hours before kick-off, and with a genuine Ibrox-day atmosphere that spills out onto the forecourt.

restaurants.name: Ox and Finch
restaurants.description: Sharing plates, impeccable sourcing, and one of the best wine lists in Scotland. The standout destination restaurant in Glasgow for a pre-match dinner. Book well in advance for match weekends.

restaurants.name: Ubiquitous Chip
restaurants.description: Glasgow's most iconic restaurant — four decades of Scottish cooking, a covered courtyard, and a wine list that has defined the city's restaurant culture. The upstairs brasserie is more affordable than the main restaurant. An essential Glasgow experience.

restaurants.name: Paesano Pizza
restaurants.description: The best pizza in Scotland, consistently. Neapolitan-style, wood-fired, queue-only — but the queues move fast and the pizza is genuinely excellent. Perfect for a relaxed pre-match lunch.

restaurants.name: Cail Bruich
restaurants.description: Glasgow's Michelin-starred restaurant — modern Scottish fine dining on Great Western Road. For a special occasion dinner the night before a big match, this is the booking to make.

postMatch.name: The Horseshoe Bar, Drury Street
postMatch.description: Glasgow's most famous old pub — the longest continuous bar in Britain, apparently — and an institution for post-match drinking in the city centre. Traditional, busy, and brilliantly Glasgow.

postMatch.name: Sub Club, Jamaica Street
postMatch.description: One of Britain's legendary underground clubs — the long-running Subculture night on Saturdays has been running since 1987. If you're staying over after a Saturday match and want a proper night out, this is the destination.

postMatch.name: Ashton Lane
postMatch.description: A cobbled Victorian lane in Hillhead lined with bars and restaurants — one of Glasgow's most atmospheric evening destinations. The Ubiquitous Chip, Jinty McGinty's, and the Vodka Wodka bar all open onto it. Perfect for a post-match wander.

gettingAround.fromAirport: Glasgow Airport (GLA) is 8 miles west of the city centre. The Glasgow Airport Express bus (Service 500) runs every 10 minutes to Buchanan Bus Station in the city centre (journey time around 25 minutes, £8 single). Taxis take 20-30 minutes and cost around £25-35. There is no rail link from the airport to the city centre. For Prestwick Airport (PIK), the train to Glasgow Central takes around 45 minutes.
gettingAround.fromStation: Glasgow has two main stations — Central and Queen Street — both in the city centre and connected to the Subway (underground). From Central station to Ibrox: take the Subway (Circle line) to Ibrox station, 5 minutes. From Central to Celtic Park: bus from the city centre (Argyle Street) takes around 20-25 minutes, or taxi around 15 minutes. Queen Street handles trains to Edinburgh, Stirling, and the Highlands.
gettingAround.betweenStadiums: Celtic Park and Ibrox are roughly 4 miles apart — not walkable on match day. The most practical route is subway from Ibrox station to the city centre (5 minutes), then bus or taxi to Celtic Park (15-20 minutes). Taxis between the two stadiums on a normal day take around 15-20 minutes and cost around £10-15. On Old Firm match day, travelling between the two grounds is not recommended — attend one match, not both.
gettingAround.localTransport: Glasgow's Subway — nicknamed the Clockwork Orange for its circular route and distinctive carriages — is simple, cheap, and excellent for getting between the city centre and Ibrox. Buses cover the rest of the city including routes to Celtic Park. Taxis are plentiful and affordable by UK city standards. The First Bus app is useful for real-time information on Glasgow's bus routes. Walking is viable within the city centre and West End — Glasgow's grid-plan centre is navigable on foot.

beyondFootball.name: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum
beyondFootball.description: One of the finest free museums in Britain — the collection spans everything from Dalí's Christ of Saint John of the Cross to a full-size Spitfire suspended from the ceiling, from Charles Rennie Mackintosh to a Benin bronze. The building itself, a terracotta baroque palace in Kelvingrove Park, is extraordinary. Give it a full morning.

beyondFootball.name: The Necropolis
beyondFootball.description: A Victorian cemetery on a hill overlooking Glasgow Cathedral — the most spectacular and atmospheric urban cemetery in Scotland. The monuments to Glasgow's Victorian industrialists are extraordinary, the views over the city are remarkable, and the whole place has a peculiar, compelling grandeur. Free to enter, and unmissable.

beyondFootball.name: The Clyde Waterfront Walk
beyondFootball.description: The regenerated Clyde waterfront traces the bones of Glasgow's greatest industry — the shipyards that once launched ships for half the world's navies. The Riverside Museum (another free entry, spectacular building by Zaha Hadid) sits at the western end. The Tall Ship moored outside is the last of Glasgow's sailing ships still floating.

beyondFootball.name: Charles Rennie Mackintosh Trail
beyondFootball.description: Glasgow's greatest artist designed buildings across the city that remain among the finest examples of Art Nouveau architecture anywhere in Europe. The Scotland Street School Museum, the Willow Tea Rooms, and the Glasgow School of Art (partially restored after a devastating fire) are the key stops. The Hunterian Art Gallery on the University campus has the most complete collection of his furniture and interiors.

beyondFootball.name: Ashton Lane and the West End
beyondFootball.description: On a Friday or Saturday evening, the cobbled lane of Ashton Lane in Hillhead is the most atmospheric place in Glasgow — bars spilling light, a cinema at the end, the Victorian tenements above. Walk up Byres Road from Hillhead subway station, turn left into Ashton Lane, and follow your nose.

beyondFootball.name: Day Trip to Loch Lomond
beyondFootball.description: The southern shore of Loch Lomond is 30 minutes from Glasgow city centre by train. If you're staying for the weekend, the scenery of the first Highland loch is an extraordinary contrast to the urban intensity of the city. Balloch is the closest town; Luss, further up the west shore, is one of Scotland's prettiest villages.

insiderTips: Old Firm tickets are almost impossible to obtain without a club membership — both Celtic and Rangers allocate almost entirely through their own supporter schemes. Don't bother with touts (prices are extreme and fake tickets circulate). A non-Old Firm fixture at either ground still delivers exceptional atmosphere with far more accessible tickets.

The Subway is the secret weapon of Glasgow transport — a single flat fare gets you around the circular route including to Ibrox station. Buy a token from the machine at any station. It runs late on match days.

Glasgow's West End is where to eat — not the chain restaurants around the city centre. Byres Road, Finnieston, and Ashton Lane have the best independent restaurants and bars in the city. Book ahead for match weekends.

Celtic Park's atmosphere is at its absolute peak for European matches — if you can time a visit to coincide with a Champions League or Europa League game at Parkhead, the noise level is genuinely extraordinary. The pre-match ritual of 'You'll Never Walk Alone' under floodlights is one of football's great spectacles.

Glasgow gets a lot of rain — pack accordingly and embrace it. The city does not shut down for weather. The pubs are warm, the people are warm, and a wet match day in Glasgow is still a great match day.

name: Leeds
description: Yorkshire's biggest city and home to Leeds United — one of England's most passionate and storied clubs.
longDescription: Leeds is a brilliant football destination and one of England's most underrated cities. Elland Road is a fortress with a wall of noise on match days — the Leeds faithful are among the most vocal in the country. The city centre has been transformed in recent years with excellent restaurants, bars, and the Trinity Leeds shopping centre. The Victoria Quarter with its stunning Victorian arcades is unmissable. It's a great city for a weekend away.

bestAreas.name: City Centre
bestAreas.description: Perfect base with shuttle buses to Elland Road. Excellent hotels and dining.

bestAreas.name: Headingley
bestAreas.description: Student area with good value hotels. Regular buses to the city centre.

name: Sheffield
description: The Steel City is home to England's oldest football clubs and a proud football heritage.
longDescription: Sheffield has a unique place in football history — it's home to the world's oldest football club (Sheffield FC), the world's oldest professional club (Sheffield United), and Bramall Lane is the world's oldest major football ground still in use. Sheffield Wednesday at Hillsborough add to the city's incredible football heritage. The city itself is lively and welcoming, with a great independent food and bar scene centred around the Kelham Island and Broomhill areas.

bestAreas.name: City Centre
bestAreas.description: Walking distance from Bramall Lane. Good range of hotels.

bestAreas.name: Kelham Island
bestAreas.description: Trendy area with craft beer bars and independent restaurants.

name: Sunderland
description: A passionate football city in the North East, home to the Stadium of Light and the famous Black Cats.
longDescription: Sunderland is one of the most passionate football cities in England. The Stadium of Light is a modern, impressive ground and the Sunderland faithful are among the most dedicated supporters you'll find anywhere. The city sits on the River Wear in the North East, with a proud industrial heritage and a warm community spirit. It's also well-positioned for exploring the North East — Newcastle is just 15 miles away.

bestAreas.name: City Centre
bestAreas.description: The best base with easy Metro access to the Stadium of Light.

bestAreas.name: Roker
bestAreas.description: Seaside suburb with guest houses and a beach. A mile from the city centre.

name: Nottingham
description: A city of remarkable football heritage — home to Nottingham Forest, two-time European Cup winners, and rivals Notts County, the world's oldest professional football club.
longDescription: Nottingham punches well above its weight as a football city. The City Ground on the banks of the River Trent is home to one of English football's greatest clubs — Nottingham Forest won back-to-back European Cups in 1979 and 1980 under the legendary Brian Clough, a feat that remains one of the most astonishing achievements in the history of the game. The city itself is lively and compact, with a strong nightlife scene centred around the Lace Market, and the leafy suburb of West Bridgford right across the river from the City Ground making an excellent base. The Peak District is within easy reach for those making a weekend of it.

bestAreas.name: West Bridgford
bestAreas.description: Leafy suburb directly across the Trent from the City Ground. Great pubs and restaurants.

bestAreas.name: City Centre / Lace Market
bestAreas.description: Historic area with excellent bars, restaurants, and a vibrant nightlife scene.

bestAreas.name: Trent Bridge
bestAreas.description: Home to the famous cricket ground and a short walk to the City Ground.

name: Wolverhampton
description: A proud West Midlands city with a rich football heritage, home to Wolves and one of England's most historic stadiums.
longDescription: Wolverhampton — Wolves to football fans — is a proud West Midlands city with a history in the game that stretches back to the 19th century. Molineux, one of English football's oldest grounds, has been substantially modernised but retains its character and generates a real atmosphere when full. The city is well-connected by rail — just over an hour from London Euston — and Birmingham is only 15 minutes away, making it easy to extend your trip. The Black Country is an area of deep industrial history, and the wider region has a lot to offer visitors willing to explore beyond the stadium.

bestAreas.name: City Centre
bestAreas.description: Walking distance from Molineux, with the best range of hotels and restaurants.

bestAreas.name: Penn
bestAreas.description: Quieter residential area with good local pubs — a short taxi from the ground.

bestAreas.name: Tettenhall
bestAreas.description: Pleasant village suburb to the west, popular with visitors looking for a quieter base.

name: Burnley
description: A proud Lancashire mill town with a passionate football culture and one of England's most historic grounds in Turf Moor.
longDescription: Burnley is one of English football's great small-town clubs — a founding member of the Football League, with a loyal fanbase and a ground that carries the history of a century and a half of football. Turf Moor sits in the heart of the town, surrounded by terraced streets, and attending a match here feels genuinely authentic in a way that's increasingly rare in the Premier League. The surrounding Lancashire countryside is beautiful — the Pennines and Forest of Bowland are accessible for those making a proper trip of it. Manchester is 50 minutes away by train, making Burnley easy to combine with a broader visit to the North West.

bestAreas.name: Town Centre
bestAreas.description: Walking distance from Turf Moor, with the best selection of pubs and places to eat.

bestAreas.name: Padiham
bestAreas.description: Nearby village with a quieter feel and good local pubs.

name: Bournemouth
description: A beautiful south coast resort town with seven miles of sandy beach, and home to one of the Premier League's great underdog clubs.
longDescription: Bournemouth is one of England's finest seaside towns — seven miles of sandy beach, a mild climate that earns it the nickname the 'English Riviera', and a vibrant town centre with excellent restaurants, bars, and shops. Attending a Bournemouth match combines one of the Premier League's most intimate stadiums with a genuinely lovely destination — you can walk the pier on Saturday morning, watch the match in the afternoon, and dine in style in the evening. The Dorset countryside surrounding the town is spectacular, with the Jurassic Coast (a UNESCO World Heritage Site) and Poole Harbour among the highlights. It's one of the Premier League's most genuinely enjoyable away trips.

bestAreas.name: Town Centre
bestAreas.description: Best range of hotels, restaurants, and nightlife. 30-minute walk from the Vitality Stadium.

bestAreas.name: Boscombe
bestAreas.description: Closest area to the Vitality Stadium, with a good range of pubs and takeaways.

bestAreas.name: Southbourne
bestAreas.description: Quieter coastal suburb with a village feel and easy beach access.
